title: Draft Opposition to Motion for Summary Judgment in BSA/AML Whistleblower Retaliation Case

blind.coverage: I read all 59 criteria and the instructions. I read these documents in full: the defendant's MSJ brief and SUMF, both Hargrove-Caldwell emails, the Prescott April 18 email, the Thornburg declaration, the termination letter, Handbook § 7.4, the PIP, the 2023 business plan, the 2022 review, the Caldwell deposition excerpts, the Prescott deposition excerpts, and the Medina declaration. I read the internal audit report through § 6. I searched the Redmond expert report for the opinions the criteria rely on (7 of 9 red flags, "facially inadequate," "no reasonable compliance officer," the 14-day investigation, and the SAR violation). I also searched the record for consolidation, FDIC, and DOL-exhaustion facts. I checked every date calculation against the record (13, 32, 99, 22 and 23 days) and all are correct. I verified from primary text in this session: the repeal of 31 U.S.C. § 5328 (uscode.house.gov and LII); § 1514A(a), including the subsidiary/consolidated-statements language, and § 1514A(d) (LII); Lockheed Martin v. ARB, 717 F.3d 1121 (10th Cir. 2013), which applies the contributing-factor framework to SOX (CourtListener); and Lawson v. FMR, 571 U.S. 429 (CourtListener), which is a contractor holding and mentions subsidiary coverage only in describing the Dodd-Frank amendment. For § 5323(g), I saw the (g)(5) rights-retained clause and part of the (g)(1) prohibition quoted verbatim; the enforcement/180-day and 42121(b) provisions came back as a fetch summary, not verbatim text. I did not read Martin Marietta v. Lorenz, Crawford Rehab v. Weissman, or any Colorado case on the statutory-remedy bar to the public-policy tort. I also did not check Judge Jackson's practice standards on the format of summary-judgment responses. I noted but did not flag minor record inconsistencies that do not change what a correct answer is. These include the Thornburg declaration being executed April 22, 2024 yet shown as an exhibit at the March 8, 2024 deposition, the email timestamps and wording differing between Exhibit 5 and Caldwell's reading of it, "Amanda" versus "Diane" Prescott, and mismatched employee IDs.

findings.title: BSA claim is framed under 31 U.S.C. § 5328, which was repealed effective Jan. 1, 2021, before any of the 2023 events
findings.explanation: C-051 passes only if the brief addresses the claim 'under 31 U.S.C. § 5328', and C-037's title ties the prima facie case to § 5328. The AML Act of 2020 (Pub. L. 116-283 § 6314(b)) repealed § 5328 and replaced it with 31 U.S.C. § 5323(g). Every event here happened in 2023, so the rubric treats a repealed statute as live law and rewards briefs that do the same. The record carries the same error (the MSJ and SUMF plead § 5328), but the rubric builds on it instead of flagging it. A careful brief that re-anchors Count I to § 5323(g) (for example, 'Plaintiff's AML/BSA whistleblower claim, properly analyzed under § 5323(g)') could fail a literal reading of C-051. C-037's PASS text ('internally and to FinCEN') happens to fit § 5323(g)(1), which protects reports to supervisors, so C-037 misgrades less; its statutory anchor is still stale.

evidence.quote: PASS if the memorandum addresses Plaintiff's BSA whistleblower retaliation claim under 31 U.S.C. § 5328.
(1) retaliation in violation of the anti-retaliation provisions of the Bank Secrecy Act, 31 U.S.C. § 5328
including 31 U.S.C. § 5328, which provides administrative complaint procedures and remedies

authorities.citation: 31 U.S.C. § 5328 (Repealed. Pub. L. 116-283, div. F, title LXIII, § 6314(b), Jan. 1, 2021)
authorities.proposition: Section 5328 whistleblower protections were repealed as of January 1, 2021.
The successor AML whistleblower anti-retaliation provision covers reports to the employer or supervisors as well as to Treasury and DOJ, and runs through DOL procedures under 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b).

findings.suggested_fix: Change C-051 to 'addresses Plaintiff's BSA/AML whistleblower retaliation claim (pleaded under § 5328; governing provision now 31 U.S.C. § 5323(g))' and accept either citation. Remove '§ 5328' from C-037's title, or correct the record to plead § 5323(g).

findings.title: Rubric requires a McDonnell Douglas pretext framework, but SOX (and § 5323(g)) use the AIR21 contributing-factor standard
findings.explanation: C-046 requires three steps: prima facie case, legitimate reason, pretext. C-017 requires treating the PIP defects as pretext under a burden-shifting framework. SOX incorporates 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b): the plaintiff shows protected activity was a contributing factor, and the employer must then prove by clear and convincing evidence that it would have acted the same way. There is no pretext step. The Tenth Circuit applies this in Lockheed Martin, and the successor BSA provision imports the same burdens. The strongest opposition would say Defendant applied the wrong, stricter framework, invoke contributing-factor causation (where temporal proximity alone can suffice), and engage pretext only in the alternative. Such a brief can still pass through 'analogous framework' or the Colorado claim, but neither criterion ever credits the correct standard, and a literal judge could fail an AIR21-centered brief. C-038 correctly uses 'contributing factor', so the rubric is internally mixed.

evidence.quote: identifying the steps: (1) plaintiff's prima facie case, (2) defendant's legitimate reason, and (3) plaintiff's showing of pretext
(protected activity, employer knowledge, adverse action, and contributing factor/causal connection)

authorities.citation: Lockheed Martin Corp. v. Admin. Review Bd., 717 F.3d 1121 (10th Cir. 2013)
authorities.proposition: A SOX § 1514A claimant must show protected activity was a contributing factor; temporal proximity may alone satisfy that test; the causation showing is less onerous than under Title VII.
SOX actions are governed by the burdens of proof in 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b).

findings.suggested_fix: In C-046, accept either McDonnell Douglas or the AIR21 contributing-factor / clear-and-convincing framework, and credit a brief that argues AIR21 governs the federal claims. In C-017, allow 'pretext or failure to meet the employer's same-decision burden'.

findings.title: SOX subsidiary criterion omits the consolidated-financial-statements condition and treats Lawson as subsidiary authority
findings.explanation: C-027 says SOX 'extend[s] to employees of subsidiaries of publicly traded companies.' Section 1514A(a) covers only a subsidiary 'whose financial information is included in the consolidated financial statements' of the public parent, so the statement is materially incomplete. The record has no direct evidence of consolidation, although wholly owned status makes it a strong inference. C-028 rewards citing Lawson v. FMR for subsidiary coverage. Lawson held that SOX covers employees of contractors; it mentions subsidiary coverage only when describing the 2010 Dodd-Frank amendment, and the Lawson plaintiffs worked for subsidiaries of a private company. Because C-028 also accepts the statutory text, correct briefs pass. The defect is that the criterion rewards a weak citation and never requires the element Defendant would attack.

evidence.quote: because SOX protections extend to employees of subsidiaries of publicly traded companies
(15 U.S.C. 78o(d)) . . . may discharge, demote, suspend

authorities.proposition: Coverage includes 'any subsidiary or affiliate whose financial information is included in the consolidated financial statements of such company'.

Held that § 1514A protects employees of contractors of public companies; it describes the Dodd-Frank amendment as extending protection to public-company subsidiaries but does not decide subsidiary coverage.

findings.suggested_fix: Add the consolidated-financial-statements condition to C-027 (for example, 'a wholly owned subsidiary whose financials are consolidated into RDFG's'). In C-028, make the amended statutory text the primary authority and describe Lawson as describing, not holding, subsidiary coverage.

Still, a careful brief that hedges on Westlake and Meridian because of the mismatch, or calls the audit only 'undercutting' rather than contradicting the PIP, could fail a strict reading.

**4.2 Westlake Commercial Properties LLC (Loan No. CL-2020-05537)**
Q. All three? A. Yes.

findings.suggested_fix: Make the account names and loan numbers match across the PIP, the audit, and the MSJ, or have C-013 accept briefs that rely on Caldwell's concession and note the naming discrepancy.

findings.title: C-040's PASS and FAIL tests measure different things (10 distinct documents vs. 10 citations)
findings.explanation: PASS requires 'at least 10 distinct document citations', meaning ten different documents. FAIL is triggered by 'fewer than 10 record citations', which counts citations. A brief with 25 record citations to 8 documents meets neither condition, so the two judges may split. The count of ten is also an arbitrary threshold the instructions never stated. With 15 documents available, most thorough briefs will clear it, so this is minor.

evidence.quote: with at least 10 distinct document citations across the brief. FAIL if the memorandum contains fewer than 10 record citations to specific documents.

findings.suggested_fix: Use one test in both branches, for example 'cites at least 10 distinct record documents; FAIL if fewer than 10 distinct documents are cited'. Alternatively, replace the count with 'factual assertions are supported by pinpoint record citations throughout'.

findings.title: Record's filing date makes both federal whistleblower claims facially premature under DOL exhaustion rules
findings.explanation: The SUMF says the lawsuit was filed November 17, 2023, 56 days after the September 22 termination. SOX, § 1514A(b)(1)(B), permits a district-court action only if DOL has not issued a final decision within 180 days of the administrative complaint. The successor BSA provision, § 5323(g), has the same 180-day DOL kick-out. On these dates, neither federal claim could properly be in district court. Defendant did not raise exhaustion, and a plaintiff's opposition would not volunteer it, so the criteria do not misgrade the opposition directly. But the rubric's federal-claim criteria rest on a scenario whose own dates undercut them, and a careful solver may spend effort on, or hedge about, an issue the rubric ignores.

evidence.quote: prior to the filing of this lawsuit on November 17, 2023
your employment with Ridgeline National Bank is terminated effective September 22, 2023

authorities.proposition: SOX retaliation claims proceed first before the Secretary of Labor, with district-court kick-out available only after 180 days without a final decision.
AML whistleblower claims are filed with the Secretary of Labor, with district-court action if no final decision issues within 180 days.

findings.suggested_fix: Change the lawsuit filing date (and case number year) in the record to a date consistent with a DOL filing followed by a 180-day kick-out, or state in the record that exhaustion was satisfied.

blind.overall: Most of the rubric is sound and well grounded in the record. The fact-based criteria are all supported: the Hargrove email, the 13/32/99/22/23-day intervals, the $10M vs. $15M target, the Thornburg declaration, the Orion complaint, the Whitfield/Lomax comparison, Medina and Gunther, Prescott's testimony, and Redmond's opinions. The main defect is legal. The BSA claim is anchored to 31 U.S.C. § 5328, which was repealed effective January 1, 2021 and replaced by § 5323(g), and C-051 explicitly requires the § 5328 framing. Relatedly, the rubric requires a McDonnell Douglas pretext structure even though SOX, and the successor BSA provision, use the AIR21 contributing-factor / clear-and-convincing framework. The rubric therefore never credits the correct standard and could penalize the stronger brief. Smaller issues: the SOX subsidiary criterion omits the consolidated-financial-statements condition and leans on Lawson; the audit and PIP loan identifiers do not match; C-040's PASS and FAIL tests measure different things; and the record's filing date makes the federal claims facially premature. Under the all-pass metric, C-051 and C-046 are the criteria most likely to fail a legally sophisticated answer.

sol_verdicts.reason: §5328 was repealed effective Jan. 1, 2021. Sol's carve-out point also holds, and it reaches the repealed statute too: old §5328(e) and current §5323(g)(6) both exclude employers subject to 12 U.S.C. §1831j, which covers insured depository institutions, and the record calls Ridgeline a 'nationally chartered commercial bank'. C-037 rewards a BSA prima facie case, with internal reports as protected activity, that fails under either version. C-051 only asks the brief to address the claim as pleaded, so the misgrade risk there is low.

The MSJ § E expressly argues field and conflict preemption, so a rebuttal is required. The propositions the criteria reward are correct: neither statute expressly preempts state law, and §1514A(d) and §5323(g)(5) preserve state remedies. Colorado's adequate-statutory-remedy doctrine is a separate argument that none of these criteria forbids. A brief that also answers the Crawford/Martin Marietta point still passes. The criteria are incomplete, but they do not misgrade.

SOX incorporates the AIR21 burdens in 49 U.S.C. §42121(b): contributing factor, then the employer's clear-and-convincing same-action defense. There is no pretext step. The Tenth Circuit applies this in Lockheed Martin, and Murray v. UBS confirms no retaliatory-intent element. C-046 and C-017 require a pretext structure and never credit the AIR21 standard, but the Colorado claim or 'analogous framework' language can satisfy them, so they are arguable. C-038 correctly says 'contributing factor'.

C-027 leaves out §1514A(a)'s condition that the subsidiary's financials be consolidated into the parent's statements, though wholly owned status makes consolidation a strong inference. C-028 accepts the statutory text, and citing Lawson's description of the Dodd-Frank amendment is common practice. C-038 and C-049 accept SOX protected activity. Arguing that an AML report is reasonably believed to involve wire or bank fraud is reasonable advocacy, not a rubric error.

A web search did not find FinCEN advisory FIN-2023-A001, so the advisory the Redmond report relies on may be fictional. C-048 does not depend on the advisory's identity. It rewards citing Redmond's 7-of-9 conclusion, or the 'no reasonable compliance officer' conclusion, both of which appear verbatim in the report. A brief can cite either without vouching for the advisory.

findings.title: C-037 rewards a BSA prima facie case under repealed §5328 that is also unavailable against an insured bank under either version
findings.explanation: C-037's title anchors the claim to 31 U.S.C. §5328, which the AML Act of 2020 repealed effective Jan. 1, 2021, before any of the 2023 events. Its PASS text also treats internal reports as BSA-protected. The claim fails on a second, independent ground. Old §5328(e) and its successor §5323(g)(6) both exclude any employer subject to FDIA §33 (12 U.S.C. §1831j), and Ridgeline is a 'nationally chartered commercial bank', which is insured by operation of law. Such an employee's federal banking whistleblower remedy is §1831j, which protects reports to federal banking agencies or the AG, not internal reports. Old §5328(a) also never protected internal reports. The criterion therefore rewards stating as viable law a claim that fails under both the repealed and the current statute. A careful brief that flags the defect and pivots to §1831j or SOX, instead of building the §5328 elements with internal reporting as protected activity, risks failing it.

evidence.quote: Prima facie case for BSA retaliation (31 U.S.C. § 5328) constructed
reporting suspected BSA/AML violations internally and to FinCEN
It is a nationally chartered commercial bank --- a wholly owned subsidiary of Ridgeline Financial Group, Inc.
retaliation in violation of the anti-retaliation provisions of the Bank Secrecy Act, 31 U.S.C. § 5328

authorities.citation: 31 U.S.C. § 5328 (repealed by Pub. L. 116-283, § 6314(b), effective Jan. 1, 2021)
authorities.proposition: The BSA whistleblower provision relied on was repealed before the 2023 events.
The section did not apply to financial institutions subject to FDIA § 33.
'This subsection shall not apply with respect to any employer that is subject to section 33 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1831j)'.
Insured depository institutions may not retaliate against employees who provide information to a federal banking agency or the AG. Enforcement is by a district-court action within 2 years.
National banks are Federal Reserve members and FDIC-insured.

findings.suggested_fix: Rebuild Count I around a claim that is actually available, such as §1831j (given the OCC inquiry). Alternatively, credit a brief that addresses Count I while flagging the §5328 repeal and bank carve-out. Remove 'internally' from the BSA protected-activity element.

final.changes_from_blind: I made four changes after reading Sol. (1) I adopted and verified Sol's carve-out point: current §5323(g)(6) and repealed §5328(e) both exclude employers subject to 12 U.S.C. §1831j, and the record calls Ridgeline a nationally chartered bank. The BSA claim therefore fails under either version, and C-037 rewards treating internal reports as BSA-protected, which was wrong even under old §5328(a). That makes C-037 the primary problematic criterion. (2) I downgraded C-051 to arguable, because it only asks the brief to address the claim as pleaded. (3) I dropped C-028, because it accepts the statutory text and citing Lawson's description of the amendment is common practice; C-027 stays arguable. (4) I dropped blind O6, the DOL-exhaustion filing date, because Defendant did not raise it, it does not change what a correct opposition says, and no criterion misgrades on it. I rejected Sol's Colorado preemption cluster (C-029, C-030, C-039) and its C-048 advisory point as rubric defects.
final.overall: Most of the rubric is well grounded in the record: the knowledge, timeline, pretext and comparator facts all check out. The clear defect is Count I. The rubric treats a BSA whistleblower claim under 31 U.S.C. § 5328 as viable. That statute was repealed before the 2023 events, and both it and its successor, § 5323(g), exclude employers subject to 12 U.S.C. § 1831j, which covers national banks like Ridgeline. So C-037's BSA prima facie case, with internal reports treated as protected, is wrong law under either version, and C-051 carries the stale label. Secondary issues: C-046 and C-017 require a McDonnell Douglas pretext framework and never credit SOX's AIR21 contributing-factor / clear-and-convincing standard; C-027 omits the consolidation condition for subsidiary coverage; the audit and PIP loan identifiers do not match (C-013); and C-040's PASS and FAIL counting tests differ. Under the all-pass metric, C-037 is the criterion most likely to penalize a legally careful answer.
final.coverage: I reviewed all 59 criteria and the instructions, relying on my blind-pass reading of all 15 documents. This pass I also read Sol's audit (markdown and index) and re-checked the record for Sol's points: bank charter, FinCEN/OCC facts, MSJ § E's preemption and Colorado adequate-remedy arguments, and the Redmond report's use of FIN-2023-A001. I read these primary texts this session: 31 U.S.C. § 5323(g)(1) and (g)(6) (LII); former 31 U.S.C. § 5328, including (e) (govinfo, 2011 edition); and 12 U.S.C. § 1831j(a)(1) and (b) (LII). A web search did not find FIN-2023-A001. I did not verify 12 U.S.C. §§ 222 or 1814(b) (national banks are insured) or Murray v. UBS from primary text, and I did not read Colorado cases on the adequate-statutory-remedy bar.
